          63def generate_zmq_ipc_path() -> str:
64    """Generate a unique ZMQ IPC path."""
65    # The full UUID is 36 chars (8-4-4-4-12 hex)
66    # However, this may cause the full path to be too long for ZMQ if you append
67    # additional characters to it. As such, we truncate the UUID to 18 chars.
68    # The chances of collision are still very low, because we don't really make
69    # that many ZMQs anyways.
70    short_uuid = uuid.uuid4().hex[:18]
71    base_rpc_path = tempfile.gettempdir()
72    # An ipc:// socket binds to a filesystem path bounded by
73    # zmq.IPC_PATH_MAX_LEN (107 on Linux, the sun_path limit). On hosts with a
74    # long temp dir (e.g. the BuildBuddy macOS remote-build sandbox, whose
75    # gettempdir() is ~80 chars) the base path plus a caller suffix overflows
76    # that limit. Fall back to a short, writable directory so the
77    # fully-suffixed path always fits.
78    suffix_budget = len("/") + len(short_uuid) + _MAX_IPC_SUFFIX_LEN
79    if len(base_rpc_path) + suffix_budget > zmq.IPC_PATH_MAX_LEN:
80        base_rpc_path = "/tmp"
81    return f"ipc://{base_rpc_path}/{short_uuid}"

          105    async def stream(
106        self, req_id: RequestID, data: BaseContextType
107    ) -> AsyncGenerator[tuple[list[PipelineOutputType], int | None], None]:
108        """Submit a request to the model worker and return a response generator.
109
110        Awaiting this coroutine registers an output queue for ``req_id`` and
111        puts ``data`` on the request queue (the handoff to the model worker).
112        The push is the admission gate: if the bounded request queue
113        (``Settings.max_queue_size``) has no room, :class:`RequestQueueFull` is
114        raised *immediately* (before any response is streamed and with no
115        registration left behind), so the API can shed load with HTTP 429
116        without adding latency to the rejected request. The returned async
117        generator drains responses until the request completes.
118
119        The check is a point-in-time writability probe rather than a timed
120        blocking send: connectivity is established once at startup (see
121        :meth:`wait_until_connected`), so an unwritable socket here means the
122        queue is full, not that the worker is still connecting.
123
124        The yielded lists are guaranteed to be non-empty and ordered.
125
126        Raises:
127            RuntimeError: If a queue for the given ``req_id`` already exists,
128                indicating a duplicate request.
129            RequestQueueFull: If the worker request queue is at capacity.
130        """
131        if req_id in self.pending_out_queues:
132            raise RuntimeError(
133                f"Detected multiple requests with `req_id` set to {req_id}. "
134                "This WILL lead to unexpected behavior! "
135                "Please ensure that the `req_id` is unique for each request."
136            )
137
138        # Admission gate. Probe writability and push under a lock so the probe
139        # is authoritative: a full request queue (the worker has stopped
140        # draining under load) is rejected immediately, and because only one
141        # request is admitted at a time and the worker only frees slots, the
142        # push after a positive probe does not block. (A bare non-blocking send
143        # is unsafe here: with a finite high-water mark a multipart send can
144        # accept some frames and then EAGAIN, desyncing the stream.)
145        async with self._admission_lock:
146            if not await self.request_queue.writable():
147                raise RequestQueueFull(
148                    f"Model worker request queue is full; rejecting {req_id}."
149                )
150
151            out_queue: asyncio.Queue[
152                tuple[float, SchedulerResult[PipelineOutputType]]
153            ] = asyncio.Queue()
154            self.pending_out_queues[req_id] = out_queue
155            try:
156                await self.request_queue.put(data)
157            except BaseException:
158                # Submission failed before any response streamed; roll back the
159                # registration and cancel so the worker drops partial state.
160                del self.pending_out_queues[req_id]
161                with contextlib.suppress(Exception):
162                    self.cancel(req_id)
163                raise
164
165        return self._drain_responses(req_id, out_queue)

          323async def _request_queue_full_exception_handler(
324    request: Request, exc: Exception
325) -> JSONResponse:
326    """Map a full model-worker request queue to HTTP 429.
327
328    ``RequestQueueFull`` is raised at admission (the push to the worker, awaited
329    before any response status is committed) by any endpoint that submits to the
330    worker, so it is handled centrally here rather than per route. Returns the
331    OpenAI ``rate_limit_error`` envelope with a ``Retry-After`` hint; the
332    rejection rate is observable via ``maxserve.request_count{code="429"}``.
333    """
334    assert isinstance(exc, RequestQueueFull)
335    request_id = getattr(request.state, "request_id", "<unknown>")
336    logger.warning("Request queue full for request %s", request_id)
337    return JSONResponse(
338        status_code=429,
339        content=openai_error_body(
340            429, "Server is at capacity. Please retry later."
341        ),
342        headers={"Retry-After": "1"},
343    )

          244    @traced
245    def _retrieve_pending_requests(self) -> None:
246        """
247        Retrieves pending requests from the request queue.
248
249        This method drains the request queue synchronously and processes
250        any contexts that are available.
251
252        This method is responsible for ensuring that new requests are continuously
253        fetched and made available for batching and scheduling.
254        """
255        max_items = self.max_items_per_drain
256        if self.max_pending_requests is not None:
257            # Cap M: only pull enough to keep the pending (CE/prefill) queue at
258            # or below max_pending_requests. Anything beyond that stays in the
259            # request queue, backing it up so the API can shed load.
260            available = self.max_pending_requests - len(
261                self.batch_constructor.all_ce_reqs
262            )
263            if available <= 0:
264                return
265            max_items = min(max_items, available)
266
267        with Tracer("drain_queue"):
268            items = drain_queue(
269                self.request_queue,
270                max_items=max_items,
271            )
272
273        with Tracer(f"adding_to_batch_constructor: {len(items)} items"):
274            for context in items:
275                self.batch_constructor.enqueue_new_request(context)
276                if self._tracing:
277                    parent = _parent_trace_context(context)
278                    self._prefill_spans[context.request_id] = (
279                        _tracer.start_span(
280                            "max.phase.prefill",
281                            context=parent,
282                            attributes={
283                                "max.request.id": str(context.request_id)
284                            },
285                        )
286                    )
287                    traced = (
288                        self._kernel_capture is not None
289                        and self._kernel_capture.admit(context, parent)
290                    )
291                    self._batch_links.admit(context.request_id, parent, traced)

          186def _to_numpy(self: Buffer) -> npt.NDArray[Any]:
187    """Converts the buffer to a numpy array.
188
189    If the buffer is not on the host, a copy will be issued.
190    """
191    if self.pinned or self.device.is_host:
192        cpu_buf = self
193    else:
194        cpu_buf = self.to(CPU())
195
196    try:
197        arr = np.from_dlpack(cpu_buf)
198    except RuntimeError as e:
199        if str(e).startswith("Unsupported device in DLTensor"):
200            raise RuntimeError(
201                f"Cannot convert buffer on {self.device} to numpy; move to"
202                " the host using `Buffer.to`"
203            ) from e
204        raise
205    # DLPack v0 capsules may produce read-only arrays in numpy >= 1.26.
206    # Callers expect a writable view, so return a writable copy when needed.
207    if not arr.flags.writeable:
208        arr = arr.copy()
209    return arr

          1066    def release_request(self, request_id: RequestID) -> None:
1067        """
1068        Releases a request from the batch constructor for all replicas.
1069
1070        This method searches for the given request_id in both context encoding (CE)
1071        and text generation (TG) request queues for each replica. If found, it removes
1072        the request entry and calls self.pipeline.release(request_id) to free resources.
1073
1074        Args:
1075            request_id: The RequestID of the request to be released.
1076        """
1077        if not self.contains(request_id):
1078            raise ValueError(f"Request {request_id} not found in any replica.")
1079
1080        # Grammar-gated requests are not bound to a replica yet: nothing was
1081        # claimed in the KV cache and no replica queue holds them.
1082        if request_id in self._grammar_pending:
1083            del self._grammar_pending[request_id]
1084            assert self._grammar_gate is not None
1085            self._grammar_gate.release(request_id)
1086            self.pipeline.release(request_id)
1087            return
1088
1089        # Pooled CE requests are not bound to a replica yet: nothing was
1090        # claimed in the KV cache and no replica queue holds them.
1091        if request_id in self._ce_pending:
1092            del self._ce_pending[request_id]
1093            self._ce_arrival.pop(request_id, None)
1094            self._bind_seq.pop(request_id, None)
1095            self.pipeline.release(request_id)
1096            return
1097
1098        self._ce_arrival.pop(request_id, None)
1099
1100        # Drop any cordon entry; the request's blocks are freed by the normal
1101        # release path below (its pending onload keeps them pinned until it
1102        # completes, after which poll_transfers unpins them).
1103        self._onloading_reqs.pop(request_id, None)
1104        self._readmitted_lookups.pop(request_id, None)
1105        self._lookup_holds.pop(request_id, None)
1106        self._bind_seq.pop(request_id, None)
1107
1108        bound = self._bound_requests[request_id]
1109        replica = self.replicas[bound.replica_idx]
1110
1111        if request_id in replica.ce_reqs:
1112            del replica.ce_reqs[request_id]
1113        elif request_id in replica.tg_reqs:
1114            del replica.tg_reqs[request_id]
1115        elif request_id in replica.deferred_lora_requests:
1116            del replica.deferred_lora_requests[request_id]
1117        # Request may already be in an active batch and therefore not appear in
1118        # any pending queue; continue cleanup in that case.
1119
1120        # Clean up LoRA state if no other request uses this adapter.
1121        # Note: We only check the current replica because LoRA currently requires
1122        # data_parallel_degree == 1. If DP > 1 LoRA becomes supported, this check
1123        # would need to search across all replicas.
1124        lora_name = self._request_id_to_lora_name.pop(request_id, None)
1125        if lora_name is not None:
1126            # Check _request_id_to_lora_name rather than the queues because
1127            # requests may be in the active batch (not in any queue) but still
1128            # using this LoRA adapter.
1129            lora_still_needed = (
1130                lora_name in self._request_id_to_lora_name.values()
1131            )
1132            if not lora_still_needed:
1133                replica.active_loras.discard(lora_name)
1134
1135        # Release from paged cache (scheduler manages primary KV cache lifecycle).
1136        # Guard with contains() because _return_to_request_queue() may have
1137        # already released the KV cache (e.g. during preemption) while leaving
1138        # the request in _bound_requests so it remains visible to
1139        # contains(). Without this check a subsequent release_request() call
1140        # (e.g. from a delayed overlap-scheduler response) would attempt a
1141        # second release and raise "Attempted to release request ID but it is
1142        # not claimed".
1143        if self.kv_cache is not None and self.kv_cache.contains(bound.ctx):
1144            self.kv_cache.release(bound.ctx)
1145
1146        # Pipeline release handles model-specific cleanup (e.g. vision encoder cache)
1147        self.pipeline.release(request_id)
1148
1149        if self._grammar_gate is not None:
1150            self._grammar_gate.release(request_id)
1151
1152        # _bound_requests is the source of truth for whether a request
1153        # is managed by the scheduler (checked by contains()).
1154        # Remove from here, marking the request as fully released.
1155        del self._bound_requests[request_id]

          NGINX: event-driven server architecture
          NGINX: event-driven server architecture · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          When an NGINX server is active, only the worker processes are busy. Each worker process handles multiple connections in a nonblocking fashion, reducing the number of context switches.
          Each worker process is single‑threaded and runs independently, grabbing new connections and processing them. The processes can communicate using shared memory for shared cache data, session persistence data, and other shared resources.
          The NGINX worker processes begin by waiting for events on the listen sockets (accept_mutex and kernel socket sharding). Events are initiated by new incoming connections. These connections are assigned to a state machine – the HTTP state machine is the most commonly used, but NGINX also implements state machines for stream (raw TCP) traffic and for a number of mail protocols (SMTP, IMAP, and POP3).
          The state machine is essentially the set of instructions that tell NGINX how to process a request. Most web servers that perform the same functions as NGINX use a similar state machine – the difference lies in the implementation.
          Scheduling the State Machine Think of the state machine like the rules for chess.

          HTTP Proxy: By default there is one HTTP proxy actor on the head node. This actor runs a Uvicorn HTTP server that accepts incoming requests, forwards them to replicas, and responds once they are completed. For scalability and high availability, you can also run a proxy on each node in the cluster via the proxy_location field inside serve.start() or the config file.
          Replicas: Actors that actually execute the code in response to a request. For example, they may contain an instantiation of an ML model. Each replica processes individual requests from the proxy. The replica may batch the requests using @serve.batch. See the batching docs.
          For each request in a deployment’s queue, an available replica is looked up and the request is sent to it. If no replicas are available (that is, more than max_ongoing_requests requests are outstanding at each replica), the request is left in the queue until a replica becomes available.

          libuv: design of the I/O event loop
          libuv: design of the I/O event loop · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          The I/O (or event) loop is the central part of libuv. It establishes the content for all I/O operations, and it’s meant to be tied to a single thread. One can run multiple event loops as long as each runs in a different thread. The libuv event loop (or any other API involving the loop or handles, for that matter) is not thread-safe except where stated otherwise.
          The event loop follows the rather usual single threaded asynchronous I/O approach: all (network) I/O is performed on non-blocking sockets which are polled using the best mechanism available on the given platform: epoll on Linux, kqueue on OSX and other BSDs, event ports on SunOS and IOCP on Windows. As part of a loop iteration the loop will block waiting for I/O activity on sockets which have been added to the poller and callbacks will be fired indicating socket conditions (readable, writable hangup) so handles can read, write or perform the desired I/O operation.

          Linux epoll: interest and ready lists
          Linux epoll: interest and ready lists · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          • The interest list (sometimes also called the epoll set): the set of file descriptors that the process has registered an interest in monitoring.
          • The ready list: the set of file descriptors that are "ready" for I/O. The ready list is a subset of (or, more precisely, a set of references to) the file descriptors in the interest list. The ready list is dynamically populated by the kernel as a result of I/O activity on those file descriptors.
          • Interest in particular file descriptors is then registered via epoll_ctl(2), which adds items to the interest list of the epoll instance.
          • epoll_wait(2) waits for I/O events, blocking the calling thread if no events are currently available. (This system call can be thought of as fetching items from the ready list of the epoll instance.)
          (3) A call to epoll_wait(2) is done that will return rfd as a ready file descriptor.

          Linux NAPI: network-driver event processing
          Linux NAPI: network-driver event processing · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          NAPI is the event handling mechanism used by the Linux networking stack. The name NAPI no longer stands for anything in particular [1].
          NAPI processing usually happens in the software interrupt context, but there is an option to use separate kernel threads for NAPI processing.
          napi_schedule() is the basic method of scheduling a NAPI poll. Drivers should call this function in their interrupt handler (see Scheduling and IRQ masking for more info). A successful call to napi_schedule() will take ownership of the NAPI instance.
          Scheduling and IRQ masking¶ Drivers should keep the interrupts masked after scheduling the NAPI instance - until NAPI polling finishes any further interrupts are unnecessary. Drivers which have to mask the interrupts explicitly (as opposed to IRQ being auto-masked by the device) should use the napi_schedule_prep() and __napi_schedule() calls:
          Drivers which have to mask the interrupts explicitly (as opposed to IRQ being auto-masked by the device) should use the napi_schedule_prep() and __napi_schedule() calls:
          if (napi_schedule_prep(&v->napi)) { mydrv_mask_rxtx_irq(v->idx); /* schedule after masking to avoid races */ __napi_schedule(&v->napi); }
          

          Linux DMA API: CPU, physical and device addresses
          Linux DMA API: CPU, physical and device addresses · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          I/O devices use a third kind of address: a “bus address”. If a device has registers at an MMIO address, or if it performs DMA to read or write system memory, the addresses used by the device are bus addresses. In some systems, bus addresses are identical to CPU physical addresses, but in general they are not. IOMMUs and host bridges can produce arbitrary mappings between physical and bus addresses.
          From a device’s point of view, DMA uses the bus address space, but it may be restricted to a subset of that space. For example, even if a system supports 64-bit addresses for main memory and PCI BARs, it may use an IOMMU so devices only need to use 32-bit DMA addresses.

          Linux memory-management concepts
          Linux memory-management concepts · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          The memory management in Linux is a complex system that evolved over the years and included more and more functionality to support a variety of systems from MMU-less microcontrollers to supercomputers. The memory management for systems without an MMU is called nommu and it definitely deserves a dedicated document, which hopefully will be eventually written. Yet, although some of the concepts are the same, here we assume that an MMU is available and a CPU can translate a virtual address to a physical address.
          The physical memory in a computer system is a limited resource and even for systems that support memory hotplug there is a hard limit on the amount of memory that can be installed. The physical memory is not necessarily contiguous; it might be accessible as a set of distinct address ranges. Besides, different CPU architectures, and even different implementations of the same architecture have different views of how these address ranges are defined.
          All this makes dealing directly with physical memory quite complex and to avoid this complexity a concept of virtual memory was developed.

          cpu.max A read-write two value file which exists on non-root cgroups. The default is “max 100000”. The maximum bandwidth limit. It’s in the following format:
          cpu.max.burst A read-write single value file which exists on non-root cgroups. The default is “0”. This file affects only processes under the fair-class scheduler and a BPF scheduler with the cgroup_set_bandwidth callback depending on what the callback actually does.
          memory.max A read-write single value file which exists on non-root cgroups. The default is “max”. Memory usage hard limit. This is the main mechanism to limit memory usage of a cgroup. If a cgroup’s memory usage reaches this limit and can’t be reduced, the OOM killer is invoked in the cgroup. Under certain circumstances, the usage may go over the limit temporarily.

          Python multiprocessing: spawn and process lifecycle
          Python multiprocessing: spawn and process lifecycle · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          The parent process starts a fresh Python interpreter process. The child process will only inherit those resources necessary to run the process object’s run() method. In particular, unnecessary file descriptors and handles from the parent process will not be inherited. Starting a process using this method is rather slow compared to using fork or forkserver.
          

          Uvicorn: flow control and server limits
          Uvicorn: flow control and server limits · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          Flow Control¶ Proper flow control ensures that large amounts of data do not become buffered on the transport when either side of a connection is sending data faster than its counterpart is able to handle. If the write buffer passes a high water mark, then Uvicorn ensures the ASGI send messages will only return once the write buffer has been drained below the low water mark.
          Proper flow control ensures that large amounts of data do not become buffered on the transport when either side of a connection is sending data faster than its counterpart is able to handle.
          Write flow control¶ If the write buffer passes a high water mark, then Uvicorn ensures the ASGI send messages will only return once the write buffer has been drained below the low water mark. Uvicorn will pause reading from a transport once the buffered request body hits a high water mark, and will only resume once receive has been called, or once the response has been sent.
          

          ZeroMQ ipc transport: local Unix-domain sockets
          ZeroMQ ipc transport: local Unix-domain sockets · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          The inter-process transport passes messages between local processes using a system-dependent IPC mechanism.
          The inter-process transport is currently only implemented on operating systems that provide UNIX domain sockets.
          When binding a 'socket' to a local address using zmq_bind() with the 'ipc' transport, the 'endpoint' shall be interpreted as an arbitrary string identifying the 'pathname' to create. The 'pathname' must be unique within the operating system namespace used by the 'ipc' implementation, and must fulfill any restrictions placed by the operating system on the format and length of a 'pathname'.
          on Linux only, when the endpoint pathname starts with @, the abstract namespace shall be used. The abstract namespace is independent of the filesystem and if a process attempts to bind an endpoint already bound by a process, it will fail. See unix(7) for details.
          

          NVIDIA CUDA: asynchronous execution, streams and events
          NVIDIA CUDA: asynchronous execution, streams and events · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          The concurrency is expressed via an asynchronous interface, where a dispatching function call or kernel launch returns immediately. Asynchronous calls usually return before the dispatched operation has completed and may return before the asynchronous operation has started. The application is then free to perform other tasks at the same time as the originally dispatched operation. When the final results of the initially dispatched operation are needed, the application must perform some form of synchronization to ensure that the operation in question has completed. A typical example of a concurrent execution pattern is the overlapping of host and device memory transfers with computation and thus reducing or eliminating their overhead.
          In Synchronizing CPU and GPU, the CUDA runtime function cudaDeviceSynchronize() was introduced, which is a blocking call which waits for all previously issued work to complete. The reason the cudaDeviceSynchronize() call was needed is because the kernel launch is asynchronous and returns immediately. CUDA provides an API for both blocking and non-blocking approaches to synchronization and even supports the use of host-side callback functions.
          

          NVIDIA CUDA: driver API and context address spaces
          NVIDIA CUDA: driver API and context address spaces · retrieved 2026-11-04 · Saved extract
          Previous sections of this guide have covered the CUDA runtime. As mentioned in CUDA Runtime API and CUDA Driver API, the CUDA runtime is written on top of the lower level CUDA driver API. This section covers some of the differences between the CUDA runtime and the driver APIs, as well has how to intermix them. Most applications can operate at full performance without ever needing to interact with the CUDA driver API. However, new interfaces are sometimes available in the driver API earlier than the runtime API, and some advanced interfaces, such as Virtual Memory Management, are only exposed in the driver API.
          The driver API is implemented in the cuda dynamic library (cuda.dll or cuda.so) which is copied on the system during the installation of the device driver. All its entry points are prefixed with cu.
          The driver API must be initialized with cuInit() before any function from the driver API is called.
